utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, The Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Before I invite the Defence to call its next witness, I'd first like to put on the record that on the 16th of November of this year, the Chamber was informed by the Defence that the Defence withdraws the 92 ter motion for witness Mile Dmicic and will instead call the witness viva voce, and that's what's done today through videolink. Could we start testing the videolink to see whether everything is functioning well.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning. We can hear you; we can see. Can you hear us; can you see us?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Yes, we can hear; and we can see you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Is the witness already in the videolink room or not yet?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] No, Your Honours. We will bring the witness in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And could you also inform us who else is in the videolink room.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Your Honours, apart from myself and the witness, there will be only the member of the ITSS, technical staff of the ICTY.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for that information. Could you escort the witness into the videolink room.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Dmicic, I presume. Mr. Dmicic, before you give evidence, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration, the text of which is now handed out to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Dmicic. Please be seated. Mr. Dmicic, you'll first be examined in-chief by Mr. Lukic. You'll soon see him on your screen. Mr. Lukic is counsel for Mr. Mladic. Mr. Lukic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Dmicic, good morning.

utterances.speaker: MILE DMICIC
utterances.text: Good morning to you too.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would you please be so kind to state your name for the record.

utterances.speaker: MILE DMICIC
utterances.text: Mile Dmicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would you give us your father's name?

utterances.speaker: MILE DMICIC
utterances.text: Simo.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dmicic, when were you born?

utterances.speaker: MILE DMICIC
utterances.text: On the 9th of October, 1948.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us what your profession is.

utterances.speaker: MILE DMICIC
utterances.text: I have a degree in law -- or, rather, I have a doctorate in law.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So what is it that you do nowadays?

utterances.speaker: MILE DMICIC
utterances.text: I'm a professor of constitutional law at the law school of Banja Luka university.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Before the war, the past seven or eight years, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: MILE DMICIC
utterances.text: I was an advisor, I was chef de cabinet. I was acting secretary-general and deputy secretary-general of the Presidency of the Socialist Federal Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you please give us the exact time period when you held these positions.

utterances.speaker: MILE DMICIC
utterances.text: I held these positions from 1984 until the spring of 1992, until the tragic conflicts in the region started.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who did you co-operate with then, before the war, before the conflict broke out? Give us some examples.

utterances.speaker: MILE DMICIC
utterances.text: This involved several terms of office of the then-president and Presidency of the Socialist Federal Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. So the last term of office that was from December 1990 until April 1992, that was a Presidency that had seven members. They were elected in a free general election in October 1990. It was headed by the president of the Presidency, Mr. Alija Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Have you read the "The Islamic Declaration" by Alija Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: MILE DMICIC
utterances.text: As a person who was employed in the state organs of Bosnia-Herzegovina over a longer period of time and as a person who has a degree in law and, of course, as a participant in certain professional endeavours that were not only something I had to do for my work but were also a subject of my interest in terms of my line of work, well, yes, I have read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In Bosnia-Herzegovina, did people know of the existence of "The Islamic Declaration" in 1990, 1991, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILE DMICIC
utterances.text: As for "The Islamic Declaration," as a project and programme and ideological document, and the time involved followed the well-known Sarajevo trial of 1983 onwards, that is, this well-known Sarajevo group that is linked to "The Islamic Declaration" and, of course, as for the substance and orientation and programme-based character of "The Islamic Declaration" is concerned, every well-informed intellectual was aware of its content - and how do I put this? - it would be located in the mid-19th century onwards; that is to say, everything that constitutes a synthesis of thought and activity appearing in "The Islamic Declaration" as a synthetic and comprehensive complete text of a projection, of an Islamic orientation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Could the witness answer the question now? Did people know of its existence?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MILE DMICIC
utterances.text: There should be a two-fold approach to the matter. Many of those who had this so-called Islamic radical concept of the state and society knew more about that. Those who were in the sphere of politics and societal life that we call people of secular orientation, people who belonged to the option of the then-ruling party, as well as those who were in favour of an approach based on civil life and co-existence as characterised by socialism as a social order, they knew about it to the extent to which this constituted a general framework of knowledge. Those who belonged to a collectivity of Islamic radicalism knew a lot more and, of course, that was a document that we usually call in everyday life and in professional life, a document of political, ideological programme-based or some other character which will be the basic approach to this document in the 1990s at the time when the Yugoslav Federation was disintegrating.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So how did Serbs view this document in 1990, 1991, 1992?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, before we continue, the 65 ter summary gives me the impression that the subject matter for this witness is not "The Islamic Declaration." It exclusively deals with the situation in the Republika Srpska time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There's nothing else in the 65 ter summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We informed the Prosecution, I spoke with Mr. Traldi, that I will be dealing with "The Islamic Declaration" exclusively with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's fine. But is the Chamber to play a role in this courtroom as well or is it just between the parties and that we -- I mean, 65 ter summaries are also for the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I apologise if we did not inform the Chambers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MELIKIAN
utterances.text: Yes, good morning. We were informed that the Defence would be dealing with this document but not that they would be dealing with it exclusively, just for the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If you want me to, I can deal with other documents. That's not the problem. But I don't have time, probably.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Because I gave two hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, two hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, Mr. Dmicic, how did Serbs view the document at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILE DMICIC
utterances.text: It's Serb community in Bosnia-Herzegovina, as the second largest in terms of population, primarily has an approach to this document that is based on historic memory or, rather, knowledge that is based on that, especially the wars that happened most recently before the latest tragic events in the area. Of course, there were certain fears vis-à-vis everything that is contained in "The Islamic Declaration," especially messages that are in the domain of expressing views regarding co-existence and life together in a common state, that is to say, life of the non-Islamic population. So they viewed in the view it in the context of what would happen if one of the ethnic communities in Bosnia-Herzegovina were to --

utterances.speaker: MS. MELIKIAN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Melikian.

utterances.speaker: MS. MELIKIAN
utterances.text: Yes. The answer is going well beyond the scope of Mr. Lukic's question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Although not an objection, but it's a general occurrence this morning, Mr. Lukic. Could you please take care that the witness remains within the scope of your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't think that there is anything outside the scope of my question, but it was a bit lengthy answer. Can I be directed which part is beyond my question, please, from -- my learned friend knows that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, it describes the document rather than focussing on the view, unless you say please repeat what the content of the document is. But, Mr. Lukic, let's -- to some extent, it's also not evidence which is usually given by a witness of fact. Asking how the community responds is, of course, either an expert question or requires a thorough laying of a foundation. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Dmicic, what about the Muslims in your own environment, people that you worked with? How did they view this document; for example, members of the SDA? Could you tell us briefly.

utterances.speaker: MILE DMICIC
utterances.text: We have to few the Islamic community in a two-fold manner. There are those that we can identify as supporters of that, given the prefix of radicalism. Then also there are the secular people, members of the Communist party who also viewed with fear everything that was presented from the context of the content of "The Islamic Declaration."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As for these ideas from "The Islamic Declaration," did Alija Izetbegovic first present them in "The Islamic Declaration"?

utterances.speaker: MILE DMICIC
utterances.text: It was not the first time that these ideas were presented in "The Islamic Declaration." I said at the very outset that we encounter these ideas in the world, in the mid-19th century, and then through difficult developments. However, he was the first one in 1979 to have formed this in a consistent text. And then, of course, the Sarajevo trial in 1983 - I'm going to use a legal term now - this was in some way made public. It was made a public document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we have on our screens D00557, MNA, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Melikian, could I ask you when did Mr. Lukic inform you that he wanted to make "The Islamic Declaration" part of his examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: MS. MELIKIAN
utterances.text: Yes, it was on the list of documents circulated last week, and then I believe it was yesterday morning, although I can double-check, that he spoke with Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Lukic, you know that for "The Islamic Declaration" we have a history there. The Defence failed to identify portions which they would submit. Yesterday some portions were read from that. The same remains valid, so that is, just throw the whole of "The Islamic Declaration" in is not what the Chamber expects the Defence to do, so focus on specific portions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That's our intention, just those entry questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have before us the document we'll be discussing today.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But before that, since, as you told us, you were a participant of the events that preceded the war, to the best of your direct knowledge, how did Alija Izetbegovic see the need for preserving peace in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MILE DMICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Izetbegovic, as we know, is the author of "The Islamic Declaration" from 1979. He became the president in 1990. So one should take into account that this is a period of just 11 or 12 years when he came into a situation to be able to transform the context of "The Islamic Declaration" as a programme document into a subject of his duties and responsibilities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness now answer the question, please. Witness, you told us a lot, but you didn't give an answer to the question. How did Alija Izetbegovic see the need for preserving peace in Bosnia and Herzegovina? That was the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, in answer to that question, one can briefly say this: When he came to the position of the president of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina and joining the process of searching for solutions for the entire territory of the Federation, wherein Bosnia-Herzegovina was one federal unit that he represented in those negotiations, we're talking, therefore, about his participation in the negotiations that were going on at the time. But there were three important options there. The first one, to put it most briefly, was creating a modern Yugoslav Federation, wherein Serbia, Montenegro, Macedonia and Bosnia-Herzegovina would remain, considering that from 1993, the Bosniak people were living in that entire region. There was the second option that was later abandoned; namely, in such a transformed Yugoslav state, to keep Slovenia and Croatia as well. A later option was to pursue an independent state. That option corresponds to the content of "The Islamic Declaration," if you consider that to be the shortest path between "The Islamic Declaration" and searching for a peaceful solution to the Yugoslav crisis at the time. Thus, Mr. Izetbegovic had a peaceful approach officially, but that was in the first part. In the second part, however, it was obvious that there was a completely different orientation, when the Bosniak and Croatian options in looking for a solution for Bosnia-Herzegovina became closer together. That's when the other ethnic communities, that is to say, Serbs, were becoming discriminated against and outvoted. There were, therefore, two conflicting options.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did Mr. Izetbegovic make any statements regarding peace and keeping peace in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MILE DMICIC
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Izetbegovic made a well-known statement regarding sovereignty and peace. In fact, he made a statement about sacrificing peace for the sake of creating an independent and sovereign Bosnia-Herzegovina. That is a very well-known truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I again have to urge you to keep the witness linked to your question, because the first lengthy answer of approximately three minutes wasn't an answer either to the question. It's only now when, for the third time, specifically asking about any statements, that the witness gives us a clue to what you asked him before. Could you please try to keep control.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Another introductory question: What do you know about the war past of Alija Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: MILE DMICIC
utterances.text: We can identify it best in one statement given to the television when he says that he had been convicted twice; the first time in 1946 for his participation in the Young Muslims Movement; and the second time, in the Sarajevo trial in 1983. Of course, the rest can be only discussed in the context of the tragic conflicts between 1992 and 1995 in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, could you tell us, to what extent the first and the second conviction had something to do with the war past of Mr. Izetbegovic? Let's start with 1946. Young Muslims Movement, was that related to the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, certainly, because these --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And could you in one or two lines describe what it had to do with the war.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, commonly known is the role of the Young Muslims in the context of the Second World War, their activities on the enemy side. I think that is quite sufficient as a fact. Why? Because the trial in 1946 qualified it. And that's why he was convicted and sentenced to three or four years, if I remember well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Qualified it as what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As the affiliation of the movement to the enemy side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, the 1983 trial, what had that to do with the war past of Mr. Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can associate it as a continuation of his activity and his work that is defined through "The Islamic Declaration," which was written in 1979, according to Mr. Izetbegovic himself. And, of course, the Sarajevo trial pertained to the content and his authorship of "The Islamic Declaration," together with the group that was co-accused with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If I understand you well, it's you associating "The Islamic Declaration" with the war past of Mr. Izetbegovic and not specifically the charges brought against Mr. Izetbegovic in 1983 that links to the war. Is that well understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In part, you are correct. But I'm not linking up these two actions completely. I am just saying that in terms of development through time, it is the progress of one kind of thinking that will later appear in the 1983 trial discussing this document. It's a completely legalistic approach --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- actions and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- you've answered my question. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's look at page 3 in both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We have "The Islamic Declaration" before us. We'll move through the document and try to see the development of this idea. I see in paragraphs 3 and 4 in both versions that Mr. Izetbegovic says the whole Muslim world is in a state of turmoil and changes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We do not see the right page. Interpreter's note.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It seems, Mr. Lukic that the two pages are not corresponding. Yes. Now we have corresponding pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's page 3. I asked for page 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Both page 3?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was just informed it's page 2 in English. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So it's paragraph 3 and the last sentence in this paragraph says: "[Interpretation] The era of passivity and inaction has passed forever." The next paragraph: "Everyone is trying to take advantage of this time of movement and change, particularly foreign powers, both from the east and from the west. Instead of their armies, they are now inserting their ideas and their capital, and with this new mode of influence they are once more endeavouring to accomplish their aim, to ensure their presence and keep the Muslim nations in a state of spiritual helplessness and material and political dependance."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I think the B/C/S is not on the right page. We move to the second page but this is still to be found on the previous page, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Not on this page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I see that what you were reading is above where it reads "China, Russia and the western countries." Now, I'm not that much of a B/C/S reader but "Kina and Rusija" sounds very much like China and Russia. So, therefore, I think we are on the wrong page.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No. We are on the right page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now we are because we moved one page back.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Oh, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, Mr. Dmicic, you've read this document. You've read this paper. In your view, at the time when you were working with and for Alija Izetbegovic, how did he see the relations between Muslims and foreigners? Do you have any personal knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MILE DMICIC
utterances.text: One brief conclusion can be made from all this. The basic substance of all this is fear and misgiving towards influence on processes going on in the Muslim world, whether spiritual unity will be achieved or not, the Islamic society, the Islamic order, and political independence, because the substance of this message, in fact, is who will have custody of the Muslim world? Who will have patronage over it? In that sense, he maintained very intensive communication with representatives of the international community, looking for an adequate solution within the framework of the Bosnia-Herzegovinian crisis and more generally the Yugoslav crisis, acting, of course, as the president of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina. We could say that it was a peace-seeking activity of the president. There's just one more question that is raised there. Which part of the international community dominates in these contacts? Of course, major influence was felt vis-à-vis the countries of the Islamic world. That is my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: If I look at the translation of the original, it seems that it is not a complete translation or some lines are added. If you look at the title, it's different. There is an Arabic title. I don't know what it is. But we have in English two titles. And then we have something it could be "Our goal, our motto," and then there's another line which is not translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The first part of the title we can find on the previous page in B/C/S, Your Honour, below the picture. So first two lines we would find below the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- first page of B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I just wanted to draw your attention to the fact that this translation seems not to be a translation by CLSS. It is so different in style, and when you read a portion into the transcript, it was quite different how it was translated then, or the mistakes I saw in the text itself of the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And could I take you back as well to the line below "Our goal and our motto," and that's what Judge Fluegge has drawn your attention to as well, there is one line starting with "Bismillah" and with an, what do you call it, exclamation mark at the end, that line seems not to be translated at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think that that's Arabic text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, whatever it is, but if you present this document, I take it that you'd like to know what the -- the line starting with "Bismillahirahmanirrahim" that's what I can try to -- what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then you should not present this document if you have no idea and if you want to --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's what we have, Your Honour. We have to present this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. You can ask --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Later on it will be checked. It's not that we can present the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, if you present a translation, then it should be either a translation which is complete, accurate and tested, or you draw our attention to the fact that you were unable to read certain parts of it and that, for that reason, you'll further submit it for clarification. That's how you should deal with the matter and you have done neither of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We can now -- we can propose parts of the document to be admitted, so we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- are not asking for this "Bismillahirahmanirrahim" to be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you want this page to be admitted?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then half of it untranslated for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And some parts of the pages could be redacted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It is not redacted yet. This is a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It is not. We will see at the end what will be redacted and what will be proposed and offered for admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, we'll hear what you will tender or not, and please be aware that the Chamber will not -- either you read into the record certain portions. If that's what you do, fine. We've done that yesterday; we can do it again. Or you tender any portion of it, and whatever portion you tender, please take care that we have a translation of that page. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Now we need page 4 in B/C/S and page 3 in the English version. In B/C/S version, we need paragraphs 3 to 5, and in English version, also paragraphs 3 to 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here, in paragraph 3, in "The Islamic Declaration," it says: "In this conviction we announce to our friends and enemies alike that Muslims are determined to take the fate of the Islamic world into their own hands and arrange that world according to their own vision of it." Next paragraph says that the ideas contained in the declaration are not absolutely new. And in the last sentence of that paragraph, it says: "Its novelty lies in that it seeks to promote ideas and plans into organised action aimed at their implementation. "The struggle towards new goals did not begin today. On the contrary. The history of this struggle already knows its shhada containing pages of the suffering of its victims." In his political activity, did Mr. Izetbegovic openly express the wish for conflict, or did he conceal that?

utterances.speaker: MILE DMICIC
utterances.text: One cannot draw the conclusion concerning the public declaration of the basic substance that you spoke of. Communication with the world and everything that changed within the quest for a solution to the then-Yugoslav and Bosnia-Herzegovinian crisis indicated that the spirit of this declaration is in the context of reaching an independent sovereign state of Bosnia-Herzegovina; that is to say, outside the former Yugoslav Federation, regardless of whether it would be the entire Federation or the rump Federation, as we called it, with the remains of the former Yugoslavia. It is important to recognise here that over 700 million people who belonged to the Islamic world are probably expected to create a community that will be a guarantor --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dmicic, I do apologise. Please. My question was: Mr. Izetbegovic, did he openly show that he was in favour of conflict or did he try to conceal that?

utterances.speaker: MILE DMICIC
utterances.text: He did not express it or show it openly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us now take a look at page 5 in B/C/S, page 4 in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before we move to another page, can we scroll down in the B/C/S version. I see that the footnote we see in the translation is missing in the B/C/S version, and I have no idea where the footnote I see -- yes, the penultimate line of the text. But that is missing in the original. I have no idea why the translation has additional information than the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Obviously somebody who was translating felt that it should be explained, what "shhada" means.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Somebody.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We don't know who translated this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We have discussed that already. I just wanted to draw your attention to that fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. This document was first distributed outside Bosnia because when it was printed it could not be distributed in Bosnia and Former Yugoslavia, so probably was first translated --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, is this a translation of the B/C/S original or is it an English version which may deviate from the original?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As I could see it, this is a translation of B/C/S original with some obvious additions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, which makes it a different version.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But it's not separate text. The text that was signed by Mr. Izetbegovic is translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just for my own clarification, do I understand that what's written in B/C/S is what's written by Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And who then -- what is "Jumada al-Ula, 1390"?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's what he wrote. That's how he counted years, in Islamic way. This is year of 1390, according to the Islamic calendar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And you say this Islamic -- this B/C/S text has been translated here by somebody you don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can we see the next page in English, please. But stay with the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There we have the year, 1390 as well, but for one reason or another, it's in the language used apparently. Perhaps in B/C/S that's a different wording compared to the English way of expressing that year.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's different spelling, same pronunciation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we move now to page 5 in B/C/S and page 4 in English, please. We need paragraph 6 in B/C/S version and paragraph 3 in English version. Full text in English version from the beginning of the row.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, it says here: "Every non-Islamic programme may seem to be in contrast -- every non-Islamic programme may seem to be close and within range of its target, but for the Islamic world this is pure utopia, because these programmes lie in the realm of the impossible." In your view, to what extent was Mr. Izetbegovic open to ideas that were not Islamic and based on Islam?

utterances.speaker: MILE DMICIC
utterances.text: One must always bear in mind a completely wise and prepared political leader. An Islamic order is possible only when one people, one ethnic community, has domination. However, the essence of this is much broader. It has to do with later deliberations in "The Islamic Declaration" about the possibility or, rather, impossibility of co-existence with non-Islamic people, a non-Islamic population. That would be it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, when you are asking for the pages, we are now at e-court page 4, hard copy page 5. One of the problems is that hard copy page 2 is missing at all in the English. Earlier you referred to the hard copy page numbering. So it's a bit confusing, but I think we are now reading from e-court page 4, hard copy page 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I was following e-court pages, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, earlier --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't know how that mistake happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Earlier you referred to hard copy pages. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We need again page 5 in B/C/S but now paragraphs 7 and 8, and page 4 in English, paragraphs -- paragraph --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the word "uvod" which appears on the top of this page, is that translated or -- I don't know --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I cannot see it on this page in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, on the page that was still on our screens.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think the word "uvod" appears on top of the first page where the following text is, "Do we want the Muslim peoples to break out of the crisis?" That's at least I see that the -- it's immediately following the year, which is in the B/C/S original, the previous page, and then the word "uvod" - I don't know what it means - but apparently is not translated. Do you know what it means?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Introduction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Introduction. Okay. Fine. Well, this is not an official translation, but at least I have now an idea what I'm missing. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the last page in English version on this page, we will have to move to the next page when we finish this part, and then in B/C/S version, it's somewhere in the middle of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "History demonstrates one fact: Islam is the single idea which has been able to excite the imagination of the Muslim people" --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we move in English to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It's already there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Top of the page then.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "No other ideal, foreign to Islam, has ever managed to hold sway in any meaningful way either in culture or at state level. All that is great and noteworthy in the history of the Muslim peoples has been done under the banner of Islam. Only a few thousand tried warriors of Islam forced Britain to withdraw from Suez in the 1950s, while the combined armies of the Arab nationalist regimes are now, for the third time, loosing the battle against Israel. Turkey, as an Islamic country, ruled the world. Turkey as a plagiary of Europe, is now a third-rate country." Further down it says: "A Muslim can die only in the name of Allah and for the glory of Islam or flee from the battle-field." How did Alija Izetbegovic view Islamic countries that espoused western democracy?

utterances.speaker: MILE DMICIC
utterances.text: If one carefully analyses the content in that part, it is understandable that one gains the impression that western democracies are not being accepted because they spoil Islam. Thereby, the very core in the application of this content is that Bosnia-Herzegovina should be organised as a society in which the interest of Islam would be protected.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now we need page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, it's time for a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's break time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, we'll take a break of 20 minutes, and we'd like to see you back after that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you have now spent one hour on a matter which was not announced to us. It was chaotic, to say the least. It elicited expert witness where this witness is not presented as an expert. To some extent, it's calling for an exiguous of texts rather than for factual knowledge of the witness. The Chamber expects you after the break to continue with the announced evidence which is about Republika Srpska and what the witness can tell us about that. If any time remains at the end, that is, before you have consumed your two hours, then you still have an opportunity to continue this line of questioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to continue with "The Islamic Declaration." If you want to prevent me from examining this witness, you can do that, I know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- but he --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, the examination of witnesses --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You are trying to prevent us from putting this document into evidence from the beginning of this trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, this is my last warning: If you interrupt me again, you will have to ask co-counsel to come in to replace you. Is that clear to you? Mr. Lukic, examination of witnesses is under the supervision of the Chamber. This was a non-announced 65 ter subject. As I said before, you're eliciting evidence which is not evidence elicited by a witness of fact. It is calling for exiguous. Further, it is at a level of relevance which is so low that the Chamber hereby instructs you to first address the other matters on the 65 ter list, and if any time remains, you can fill the remaining time to continue with what has turned out to be, until this very moment, evidence characterised by what I said earlier and, apart from that, presented in a chaotic way.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic. Mr. Lukic, think it over during the break. This is our instruction. We take a break and we resume at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic, I briefly respond to what you said. Page 25, line 5, you said: "You are trying to prevent us from putting this document into evidence from the beginning of this trial." Mr. Lukic, this Chamber firmly rejects any such allegation. We invited the Defence to select the portions which it wished to tender into evidence. We had no follow-up on that. This Chamber has never, never obstructed in any way that you present a witness who will deal with "The Islamic Declaration" but what you're doing today is to present - and it's not for the first time - a B/C/S version of "The Islamic Declaration" with another version in English which certainly not is a complete translation. You present this through a witness who is presented as a witness of fact, although he's invited to give his opinion about many of these things. That is what happened. This Chamber, not now, not in the past, not in the future, will in any way, in any way make it more difficult for you to have "The Islamic Declaration" in evidence. But do it, present it, in the appropriate way. That's one. Second, I must admit that I missed the word on page 6, you said: "We informed the Prosecution, I spoke with Mr. Traldi, that I'll be dealing with 'The Islamic Declaration' exclusively with this witness." Now I do understand, I missed that word, "exclusively". By the way, it also means that where you had not informed the Prosecution that you would exclusively deal with "The Islamic Declaration" that they had to prepare for what was still in the 65 ter summary, which is an inappropriate way of communicating, because the Prosecution would have saved its time by not dealing with the other matters where you exclusively wished to deal with "The Islamic Declaration" but you only announced, if I understood Ms. Melikian well, that you would deal with it, not that you would deal exclusively with it. I also am aware now that where you do not want to tender any other evidence, that this is the only thing you have remaining, where I invited you to deal with the other matters in your 65 ter -- found in the 65 ter summary; therefore, whereas, I had consulted my colleagues that you could not go on as you did, that is, in chaos and presenting expert evidence through a witness of fact, that remains valid. And I -- just give me one second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Although we were not unanimous, we will give you the full hour remaining, the Chamber allows you, within the limits I set, to continue to examine this witness in relation to "The Islamic Declaration." At the same time we have great doubts as to whether that can be done on the basis of this English version of the document. I leave it to that. And we'll stop you exactly after two hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I just may add one thing. CLSS does not translate books, so we have to use the translation we have. They --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, whenever you seek the assistance of the Chamber, you get everything you need. You know that. Whether it's what other states should provide, whatever -- whatever is there. If that causes you a problem, first of all, make clear to the Chamber in court that you're working on the basis of an English version which is not exactly the same. You had not spent a word on it, let alone that you would have asked us in advance to get that translation. Whether we could find, whether there is perhaps elsewhere a published English translation which is more accurately following the B/C/S version, not on the day of the testimony, in chaos, with a witness of fact. I leave it to that. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I just want to remind you of your guidance you gave me on page 9 from line 5 that I should focus on specific portions, so that's why I'm going through specific portions and all my questions were --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But one of my concerns was not to elicit an exiguous of this text from the witness. That's for experts. Ask him questions which a witness of fact can answer. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Dmicic, my questions so far have been and will continue to elicit your personal experience and knowledge regarding the speeches, the actions, and the conduct of Mr. Izetbegovic while you worked with him. The Chamber does not wish to listen to expert opinion, especially since you have not been announced as such, so please concentrate on your personal knowledge. Let us look at page 17 in B/C/S and page 23 in English, please. Second paragraph in B/C/S, last sentence. The last paragraph in English and it continues on the next page. Sorry, paragraph 2 in English. This sentence reads, after a certain introduction: "Whoever rises against Islam will not reap anything but hatred and resistance." I would like to know, were you ever present when Mr. Izetbegovic threatened with terrorism?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can you show us where he threatens with terrorism, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's paragraph 2, Your Honour, on this page, last sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which deals with hatred and resistance. That's terrorism? That's the same?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No. I'm asking this witness if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then you are leading the witness by drawing his attention to this portion of the document and then translating and relating this to terrorism. That's leading, Mr. Lukic, and it's even leading very much. You could have asked this question without even pointing to "The Islamic Declaration," because you're asking for the personal experience of this witness. And then if you want to relate that later to the document, that's the non-leading way of introducing this. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You've heard that I did not put my question very artfully. Do you have any comment on this last sentence by Mr. Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the microphone of the counsel be switched off.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you are asking me for an answer, yes or no, if somebody rises against Islam, the answer can only be that I have not had the opportunity to hear such public statements. This could perhaps be turned only in one context, that is so say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The question is answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You've answered my question. You were not present. Have you ever heard anything said by Mr. Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: MILE DMICIC
utterances.text: No, no, I haven't heard any such thing in public.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On the same page, 17 in B/C/S and 23 in English, the last paragraph in English, the fourth paragraph in B/C/S, Mr. Izetbegovic says in this paragraph, he talks about the liberation of Turkey from Greece, the heroic resistance in Libya during Italian occupation, the recent example of the battle against English over Suez, the war for the liberation of Algeria, for the preservation of Indonesia, and for Islamic influence in Pakistan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's on the next page, I take it. Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your direct knowledge from talking to people from the Party for Democratic Action and the SDS and any conversations you might have had with Mr. Izetbegovic? How did he see the struggle of other countries for Islam?

utterances.speaker: MILE DMICIC
utterances.text: Since I worked in the Presidency, an organ that then represented our federal unit, there was no such talk during the sessions. Whether there was such discussions with international or national officials in the Party for Democratic Action, I don't know. I see this passage as part of a tendency that occurred 16 or 17 times in the conclusion of the Presidency, that young men from the Bosniak and Croatian communities should not be sent to the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The last part is not related to your question, but if you have never heard Mr. Izetbegovic to express himself on either Turkey, Libya, Suez, or Algeria and Pakistan, then you could wait for the next question put to you by Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I was just going to say to you, Mr. Lukic, you just said to the witness he must try to answer your questions and you're going to ask questions of fact not opinion. Your last question was how did he see the struggle of other countries for Islam? You are seeking his opinion, how he sees --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If he heard him telling --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's a different question. How did he see is one thing; have you ever heard him say something is quite another.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But at --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're asking for fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But at least his answer was artful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm talking about your question. Okay. Maybe sure that your questions are formulated in such a way that you elicit facts from the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Next question, please, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So we continue on page 17 in B/C/S and page 24 in English, in e-court. In the B/C/S version, it's the last paragraph; in the English, it's the second one. It says: "The clear feelings of the Muslim masses need a thought that would move them and direct them." The last sentence in this paragraph says: "That can only be the Islamic thought." What did you see? In which way did Mr. Izetbegovic, as the number one man of the largest Muslim party, convey messages and govern that part of the population of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MILE DMICIC
utterances.text: The specific characteristic that appears in this, namely, when a certain person is, at the same time, the presiding member of a state organ and the leader of a political party - in this case, the SDA - can actually indicate that within the entire life of the republic, through the media, through political gatherings, through the involvement of certain religious organs and individuals, through changes in general conduct, through changes in language that already became customary in communicating with the Islamic world, also having the work of state organs stopped during religious holidays, perhaps in that context it is possible to give thought to the answer that this question requires.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Paragraph 3 in the English version, and we need -- and we need page 18 in B/C/S. The last paragraph in the B/C/S version on this page. In the first paragraph, we have the introduction and then the last one says: "There is only one way out. The creation and gathering of a new intelligentsia which thinks and feels in an Islamic way. This intelligentsia would then hoist the banner of the Islamic movement and, together with the Muslim masses, start action for its implementation." What did you see in practice? What happened in practice that could be reflected from this part of "The Islamic Declaration"?

utterances.speaker: MILE DMICIC
utterances.text: At the outset, I said that the impression is two-fold. Within the population and within the intelligentsia, the situation was as follows: There was a certain part of members of the academic community or elsewhere in terms of Islamic feelings and thoughts, as the declaration says, but perhaps here it primarily has to do with the following: Already then in terms of public speech, in terms of the media, publishing, and, of course, particularly through the activity of religious communities or, rather, the religious community of that people, it is something that we could call action, term it action, aimed at setting up an Islamic movement and order in Bosnia-Herzegovina. An analyst from the place where I worked can be placed within the context of this part of my answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I put a follow-up question. Sir, what is the name of this analyst you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm speaking in general terms, that is to say, carrying my own impressions. Also following headlines, titles of books, not to go into all of that, or headlines in newspapers and what leaders said -- I do apologise. They --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I have to interrupt you because I just asked you for a name. You said it is general observation. We are not so much interested in general observations but in facts. And, therefore, I would like -- if I understand you correctly, you were referring to newspaper articles, headlines and the like, and that is the basis of your knowledge for answering the last question of Mr. Lukic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, and I stand by that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. This is not really what I would like to know about. Your question, Mr. Lukic, it was, what happened in practice? And this is not an answer to your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It is not. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Dmicic, what happened in the media amongst the top people in the media? Were there any changes at the helm at the time? What happened? Sarajevo Oslobodjenje.

utterances.speaker: MILE DMICIC
utterances.text: It is hard now to go back to the identification of individual names. However, there are three main political parties that appeared on the scene then. Of course, since they are protagonists of power, then in the public media, in publishing houses, in institutions that are of public interest, each and every one of them wanted their own people to come to the helm. Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, I stop you again. It goes exactly in the same direction as we earlier said it should not go. Do you know of any change, other people coming to the helm, where, when, who? If you could tell us, we'd be interested to hear.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot identify names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, next question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Can we see page 19 in B/C/S and page 25 in English, please. [Interpretation] Second paragraph in both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We see what is written there. I quote: "The briefest definition of the Islamic order defines it as the unity of religion and law, upbringing and power, ideal and interest, the spiritual community and the state, willingness and force." Did you have an opportunity to see whether this was being carried out in practice; and, if so, in which way.

utterances.speaker: MILE DMICIC
utterances.text: My statement in relation to your question should be viewed in the context of the duties I carried out in the Presidency of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It was not a parliamentary organ that proposed bills, as well as other measures that have to do with the definition of Islam as an order and its implication, for example, in the field of legislation, that was passed at the time and that was in force. Because this period --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness. Witness, I stop you there. I'll stop you there. Could you give us facts which, in your view, are an expression of what was just read to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the very definition that appears here, the unity of faith and law, and not to go into all the rest, says --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I was asking about facts. Could you please first give us the facts you have on your mind, and then tell us how and why you consider them to be an expression of what is written here in relation to the definition of the Islamic order?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is hard to give an answer to that question, both in terms of the time involved, the functioning of the Presidency, when I was carrying out certain duties there. It is possible to present some of the facts that would be an answer to this question in terms of identifying facts. I'm speaking about a general approach. Probably --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness. Witness, give us facts. That's what I'm asking are you for, not further explanation of why it is difficult or why you, nevertheless, rather than giving facts would rely on general observations. Could you please give us the facts which reflect what is written here, in your view?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is hard from the context of this question to give the facts that you are speaking of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then listen carefully to the next question Mr. Lukic will put to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will try.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did Alija Izetbegovic have a permanent position regarding what Bosnia-Herzegovina should look like? Should it be divided, centralised, non-centralised?

utterances.speaker: MILE DMICIC
utterances.text: These are three approaches.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Please tell us about the approaches that he had.

utterances.speaker: MILE DMICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I mean Alija Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: MILE DMICIC
utterances.text: Yes. The first one had to do with remaining within the rump Yugoslav Federation, that is to say, an all-embracing, united Bosnia-Herzegovina. The second approach was the creation of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: He answered that in the first session of today, the three versions. You should put another question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When speaking of Bosnia-Herzegovina, what was his position? Did he have one? Was it a constant one? Should it be centralised, Bosnia-Herzegovina? And later on, when the war started, there were no more talks about remaining in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MILE DMICIC
utterances.text: He changed his positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was it supposed to be divided?

utterances.speaker: MILE DMICIC
utterances.text: All the time in the public and vis-à-vis the international community -- well, one should understand the crisis and solutions of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Bosnia-Herzegovina appears within the borders of the former Yugoslav state, the so-called avnoj borders --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That is not an answer to your question, please. The witness is not answering your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dmicic, you've heard this. Do you have any knowledge as to what Alija Izetbegovic's views were after the war broke out and did he stick to one position?

utterances.speaker: MILE DMICIC
utterances.text: No. Following the processes happening in Bosnia-Herzegovina, in the beginning, Bosnia-Herzegovina as a federal state, then later on, Bosnia-Herzegovina divided into these three state-forming entities, and within that, we have his government in fact, that is to say, factually. It was only part of Bosnia-Herzegovina. One should have that knowledge within the framework of this question and the answer that is now being discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So Alija Izetbegovic, was he in favour of a centralised Bosnia-Herzegovina all the time? Was he in favour of a divided Bosnia-Herzegovina all the time? Or did he change his positions?

utterances.speaker: MILE DMICIC
utterances.text: Within the framework of his view, all three approaches emerged. However, one must bear in mind that authority was exercised over a part of Bosnia-Herzegovina once it was divided after the tragic conflict started. So that is where the order that we are discussing prevailed. That is where these units were that were created --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The witness is not answering your question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh well ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me give it another try. You said after the war broke out. After the war broke out, was Mr. Izetbegovic, was he in favour of a division or was he in favour of a united Bosnia and Herzegovina? Witness. Witness, could you please answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I emphasise that throughout the war until the Dayton Accords, Bosnia-Herzegovina functioned as three states. That was in practice; whereas, Bosnia-Herzegovina was internationally recognised as a state. So Mr. Izetbegovic held out himself to be in the international community a representative of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The purpose was to keep Bosnia-Herzegovina whole, including the tendencies we've already discussed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, to make the best out of it, Mr. Lukic, you could understand the answer to be that Mr. Izetbegovic was in favour of keeping it as a whole, but there are other tendencies mentioned as well, which are not entirely clear to me. Let's try to get the questions so focussed that there is at least a chance that after a few introductions that we get an answer. And could you please start answering the question instead of giving introductory remarks. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we have page 19 in B/C/S and 25 in English, please. Are we on this page, the same page? [Interpretation] In the B/C/S, it's highlighted in the fourth paragraph, and in English, it's the last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It says: "History does not know a single truly Islamic movement that was not, at the same time, a political movement as well." Do you have any comment from practice? Have you seen such conduct in practice, while you worked in the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. What conduct, Mr. Lukic? The line reads that history has not seen ever that. Are you asking the witness whether he observed any facts in practice which would match with this observation? Is that -- that's different question from the one you asked. So could you give us any fact you observed in practice which would match with what is given here as a rather general statement about history and a political movement -- Islamic movement being a political movement at the same time? Any facts that you could match with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If one accepts the fact, my impression and my knowledge is just as I said before. We are talking about carrying out in parallel political and statesman's functions, pursuing the ideas of "The Islamic Declaration" in his political activity and in his activity as a statesman. As for facts, it is difficult to speak in such terms. This is a programme document. This is an ideological platform for political activity, and the activity was just beginning, in the early days of the conflict, while the joint Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina still functioned. The war lasted three or four years.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- after the Dayton Accords even --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, I interrupt you again. If you are talking about activity, what activity do you have on your mind which would match with this generally phrased statement in "The Islamic Declaration"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We could mention, for instance, one of his speeches, if I remember well in Bihac, which was along the lines that: All this will be translated into practice from "The Islamic Declaration" and that a large number of young people stand behind it, prepared to put this programme into practice. You can find the appropriate headlines or titles in this field. It was a huge output from the Party for Democratic Action and a large number of authors whom I won't mention now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think you have -- well, "answered the question" is perhaps a bit too much, but you at least told us that he promulgated the same ideas during a speech in Bihac, and that's a fact, a speech in Bihac, although not facts which match exactly with what was written. Next question, please, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I have one question to the witness. When did Mr. Izetbegovic deliver this speech?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't remember the date, but it was -- could it be the 1st of April, 1990? That can be checked. It's in the book published by the Party for Democratic Action, a collection of statements and speeches by the president.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. You have answered the question. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Can we have page 21 in B/C/S and 28 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We see the heading: "Islam is not just a religion." In B/C/S, it's page 26 and page 35 in English where Mr. Izetbegovic speaks about the striving of all Muslims to unite into one community, one single community. In English, it's paragraphs 1 to 3. In paragraphs also 1 and 3, in the third, it says: "One community is" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter has not found this passage yet, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's the last paragraph before "property." "Islam is the first ..." And the last sentence in this paragraph, I would read in B/C/S now. [Interpretation] "Islam is its idealogy and pan-Islamism its politics ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And now page 47 in B/C/S and 59 in English, please. We need first paragraphs in both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the first sentence already, we see "Pan-Islamism and Nationalism" is the heading, and the first paragraph begins: "In one of the arguments for the Islamic order today, we said that the tendency to gather together all Muslims in Muslim communities in the world was a natural function of the Islamic order. In today's circumstances, this striving means a struggle to create a great Islamic Federation from Morocco to Indonesia, from tropical Africa to Central Asia." Did you have occasion in reality to see with which countries Mr. Izetbegovic created the closest ties and relations?

utterances.speaker: MILE DMICIC
utterances.text: I can say that the largest number, from what I managed to find out working in the Presidency, the largest number of ties were with countries of the Islamic world. But in the Islamic Federation, reference is made to creating a federation. That means countries which do not need to be territorially linked. This was a problem --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The question was with which countries he created the closest ties. Please name the countries.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I said mainly the dominant countries of the Islamic world at the time, from Indonesia to the Middle East. Those are the countries where Mr. Izetbegovic spent some time working in certain companies of Bosnia-Herzegovina --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: To a certain extent, now you have answered the question. Please, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us look at page 22 now in B/C/S and 29 in English. In B/C/S, it's the second paragraph; in English, it's the last one.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It reads: "The first and foremost of these conclusions is certainly the conclusion about the incompatibility of Islam with non-Islamic systems. There can be neither peace nor co-existence between the Islamic faith and non-Islamic social and political institutions." This is an oft-quoted passage. I'm certain that you've heard it before.

utterances.speaker: MILE DMICIC
utterances.text: Essentially this is a striving for domination. In the circumstances of Bosnia-Herzegovina, such domination was possible only with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First of all, the question was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: There was no question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There was no question, as a matter of fact. Mr. Lukic said: "This is an oft-quoted passage. I'm certain that you've heard it before." That's an assumption. Fine. Do you seek affirmation of that assumption or would you like to add a question?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would like to add a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The gentleman started to respond so I kept silent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. You just stopped speaking, Mr. Lukic. You didn't put a question to the witness. But you now do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So, Mr. Dmicic, were there, in practice, any attitudes towards the army, the state, the institutions that would follow these lines?

utterances.speaker: MILE DMICIC
utterances.text: If you mean attitude towards institutions, it was about domination in parliamentary decision-making. It's about the attitude towards young Bosniaks joining the Yugoslav People's Army. It's about a general striving to create an independent and sovereign state. Because we are talking about 1992, a period when the circle of Yugoslavia's breakup was full and there began a search for solutions to the internal reorganisation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, in terms --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. The Party for Democratic Action, that is to say, the party of the Bosniak people in Bosnia-Herzegovina, did it create its own army before 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILE DMICIC
utterances.text: Yes, they did. It's the Green Berets --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, why do you ask a leading question?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's already in evidence in this case, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Why do we need to answer the question to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I already asked attitude toward military or toward state or ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Ask him when was the SDA formed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You've heard this, Mr. Dmicic. Do you know when the SDA was established?

utterances.speaker: MILE DMICIC
utterances.text: I think it was in 1989, one year before the multi-party elections in 1990. By that time, all the national parties were formed because they were all present at the multi-party elections in September 1990. Just after returning from --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Which one was founded first? Which national party was formed first in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MILE DMICIC
utterances.text: The SDA, that of the Bosniak people; then the HDZ, the party of the Croatian people; and then the SDS. That was formed in July of the previous year and was then was able to participate in the multi-party elections in 1990.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, although that seems to be a very repetitious of seeking of evidence, I think the order in which the parties were formed, I think we've heard it five, six, or seven times. Unless there's any specific matter. The Chamber has considered how to proceed. You'll have 15 minutes after the break. Strictly. Not one minute more. We'll take a break. We'll resume at quarter past 12.00 and you have until 12.30 to conclude your examination-in-chief. Witness, we'd like to see you back in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, your last 15 minutes starts now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We need page 22 in B/C/S and 29 in English version from this document, please. In B/C/S, it's paragraph 2. I will read in B/C/S the bolded version. In English, it's the fifth line from the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So the second part in bold letters in B/C/S says: "By claiming the right to order its own world itself, Islam obviously excludes the right or possibility of action on the part of any foreign idealogy in that area." Do you have any comment from your own practice?

utterances.speaker: MILE DMICIC
utterances.text: If Islam is an integrated system of belief, the essence of the impression pertains to the following: Activity was identical in a way in the Presidency --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could all other microphones please be switched off. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We said already at the beginning it is this unity of worldly life and religious life in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We are in a hurry so I'm going to skip a few things. Let us look at page 43 now in the B/C/S version and page 55 in the English version. It is Islamic governance that is dealt with here. We need paragraph 3 in B/C/S and it's the last paragraph in the English version. This is what it says here: "The Islamic movement should and can start to take over power as soon as it is morally and numerically strong enough to be able not only to topple the existing non-Islamic government, but also to build up a new Islamic one." How was this viewed in pre-war life in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MILE DMICIC
utterances.text: During its pre-war life, Bosnia-Herzegovina was an equitable part of the Yugoslav Federation, a federal unit with three state-forming peoples with equal rights, introducing a philosophy, morality, code of conduct, a new life, if I can put it that way, within Bosnia-Herzegovina, on the basis of the proclamations declared in this declaration are an intimation of creating a Bosnia-Herzegovina as an independent state. I point that out once again, that it had already gone through all of those stages. Building a new government means in temporal terms to wait and create conditions to ensure the domination of one or more peoples involved in a joint effort in Bosnia-Herzegovina. So we can only view this in temporal terms, that is to say, advocating the creation of conditions for toppling the existing system and creating a new one, of course, that would be based on the premises of this document. That is what I have to said.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What about the referendum and the referendum question regarding the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina? Was there a particular position on that?

utterances.speaker: MILE DMICIC
utterances.text: The referendum question is one of the worst points in the quest for a solution in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Had the compromised solution refused by Mr. Izetbegovic been adopted, then probably there wouldn't have been a war and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Again, this is opinion evidence rather than anything else, and apart from that, the facts, I think, if the witness would come to that --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: He knows the facts. He is trying to explain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, if you would not have interrupted me. The facts have reached us several times. Just from the top of my head, I can tell you it was the 15th of October and that was the assembly session which was then part left, et cetera. All those facts, I think, are well presented in the evidence. The witness started with giving an opinion. If you had asked for facts, then I might have said, isn't this repetitious evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What action did Mr. Izetbegovic take after the war in relation to the Dayton Agreement?
