utterances.speaker: MILE DMICIC
utterances.text: The Dayton Peace Agreement stopped the war and ensured the establishment and functioning of the system of the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina since the parties were not quite satisfied with the solution, but, of course, the solution did provide for peace and a continuation of normal life. As the Dayton Accords --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, I interrupt you again. The question was what action did Mr. Izetbegovic take after the war in relation to the Dayton Agreement? What action did he take; could you please tell us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In a single sentence, continuing the struggle for a centralised unitary Bosnia-Herzegovina. That is my answer in a single sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did he write any submissions; and, if so, to whom? Did he involve the constitutional court of Bosnia-Herzegovina? Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: MILE DMICIC
utterances.text: I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did Mr. Izetbegovic involve the constitutional court in the resolution of certain matters, and what happened after decisions were made? Could you please briefly just describe this to us.

utterances.speaker: MILE DMICIC
utterances.text: Even today, after 15 years, once the constitutional norm was no longer there concerning the possibility of a different --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, I'll stop you again. I'll interrupt you again. Although the question as was leading as could be, but I can ask you a leading question: Did he involve the constitutional court of Bosnia-Herzegovina? Did he, or did he not? After the war.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, because the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina as --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- an organ which --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- you don't have to explain why. Witness, you don't have to explain why. You confirmed --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I want to say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. Under the circumstances, I can interrupt you. You cannot interrupt me. You have confirmed - and that was the question - that he involved the constitutional court. Listen to Mr. Lukic's next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was the constituent quality of peoples discussed?

utterances.speaker: MILE DMICIC
utterances.text: Only two years after Dayton, Mr. Izetbegovic made a submission to the constitutional court regarding the constitutional or constituent quality of the peoples of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that led a situation throughout the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, although the entities espoused in the Dayton Accords with their subjectivity and identity were there as they were before the Dayton Accords. That would be it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was this changed subsequently? Were there any constitutional amendments? What happened?

utterances.speaker: MILE DMICIC
utterances.text: Immediately after that, the decision of the constitutional court that were made up until 2000, the High Representative, by implementing this decision, passed tens of amendments regarding the entities.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We didn't hear the end of the sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't hear the last part of your answer so please repeat it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this way, the High Representative in 2002 passed tens of constitutional amendments and fully implemented the decision of the constitutional court of Bosnia-Herzegovina, thus ensuring the constituent quality of all three peoples in the entire territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just one more question. Do you know in which way and to what extent Mr. Izetbegovic was involved in bringing in Mujahedin from Arab countries in order to wage war on the side of the Muslims in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MILE DMICIC
utterances.text: My knowledge is primarily --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please put this question now not in a five-time leading way. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know that Mujahedin came to Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MILE DMICIC
utterances.text: I know. First of all --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Both speakers are speaking at the same time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were certain persons who had connections from earlier on, and there's information to the effect that there were 10.000 of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge as to who was involved in bringing Mujahedin into Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MILE DMICIC
utterances.text: I can just say concerning a general position that these were basically persons who maintained contacts and relations with the countries that we mentioned in our previous statement; from the political and diplomatic life of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, perhaps it would assist you if I would ask the witness in what year that happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You heard the question put by Judge Orie. What year did they arrive in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Mujahedin?

utterances.speaker: MILE DMICIC
utterances.text: Our information is that it was already in 1992, particularly in 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You referred twice to information, both about the number of 10.000 and now about the years. Do I understand that you have no personal knowledge of it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We must bear in mind the fact that I was no longer on the staff of the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I lived in Republika Srpska. So territorially, I lived in a completely different area. All other information can come only from the media and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, the simple answer, therefore, is, no, I don't have that. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You don't have any personal knowledge, of course, and you told us just now why that is the case. As --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is now time for your last question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As you lived in Republika Srpska, what kind of knowledge did you acquire? Who took part in bringing in the Mujahedin?

utterances.speaker: MILE DMICIC
utterances.text: I have already said that this is knowledge but it is not facts that I could see myself. It is mainly these persons who were involved in political life or diplomatic life and had direct links to the countries that dominated in terms of co-operation with Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is to say, between 1990 and 1992, the pre-war period. That would be my answer. So this is knowledge but not facts that I could have seen directly. I mean documents and the like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, page 53, line 12, says "[Previous translation continues] ..." where I spoke. What I said is it's now time for your last question. I repeat that. You have one extra granted to you by our transcriber. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So it is good when you are not recorded in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just tell us one more thing. What are these countries with which Bosnia-Herzegovina had contacts in terms of bringing in Mujahedin and what is your knowledge in that respect? And that would be my last question.

utterances.speaker: MILE DMICIC
utterances.text: My knowledge is that this is mainly Saudi Arabia, Indonesia, and other countries that we've already mentioned within my previous statements. These are already generally known facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dmicic, thank you for having answered our questions. That is all that the Defence of General Mladic had for you for the moment. Thank you once again.

utterances.speaker: MILE DMICIC
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. Witness, Mr. Dmicic, you'll now be cross-examined by Ms. Melikian. You will see her on your screen soon. Ms. Melikian is counsel for the Prosecution, but apparently she wants to say something first.

utterances.speaker: MS. MELIKIAN
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. President. We have no questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No questions in cross-examination. Then, Mr. Dmicic, this then concludes your testimony in this court. I'd like to thank you very much for making yourself available and for having answered all the questions that were put to you. I usually say by the parties and by the Bench, but in this case I should say by the Defence and by the Bench. I wish you a safe return home again. No speaking aloud.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You are excused, Mr. Dmicic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This concludes the videolink. Is your next witness ready? Because we asked him to remain on standby the second half of the morning, and since we'll not continue with the videolink at this moment --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, but maybe it would be wise to have a short break since I have to go and pick up by my colleague Mr. Ivetic who is in the back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's fine. Then we take a bit of an earlier break. Mr. Lukic ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My problem is that if we would take the break now, that we'd have still 75 minutes to go until quarter past 2.00 and that might be too much for Mr. Mladic. So, therefore, if you could get Mr. Ivetic in two or three minutes, then we'll just wait for him. And if he rushes a bit then ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No speaking aloud, Mr. Mladic. Again. No, to no one, never. Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't know if VWS brought our next witness yet into the building, so that's why I'm not sure that we can continue immediately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that could be. Madam Registrar, could you try to find out with VWS whether the next witness is already there. Otherwise, I have a matter which we should deal with in private session anyhow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it's unclear yet whether the witness has arrived or not. Meanwhile, we'll use the time by dealing with a matter we should deal with in private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Our information is at this moment that the witness would be here in five minutes. Now, we can do two things: Either take the break now and have a little bit of a longer session. Another thing we could do is that I deal with a few procedural matters first, that we'll then continue until quarter past 1.00 or a little bit longer so that we have the full session and that we'll then hear the witness starting from five minutes from now. I think the latter would be the best so that we have no long sessions. Then I'll deal briefly with a few matters and I'd like to be informed once the witness has arrived. The first one is about Exhibit P5273 which is an excerpt from a handwritten notebook which was admitted into evidence on the 13th February of 2014. The Prosecution e-mailed the Chamber and the Defence on the 11th of November, 2015, advising that a revised English translation which includes two amendments at page 3 had been uploaded into e-court under doc ID 0672-2270-1ET. The Defence responded on the 16th of November stating that it did not object to the replacement of the translation. The Chamber hereby instructs the Registry to replace the English translation of Exhibit P5273 with the revised one of which I just read the number. The next item deals with Exhibit P7072 and is also about an English translation, a replacement. This document confirming Jandranko Palija's military service was admitted into evidence on the 28th January of 2015. At transcript pages 30815 through 30817, the Chamber identified a discrepancy between the original and the translation with regard to Palija's dates of birth. On 2nd of November, the Prosecution e-mailed the Chamber and the Defence advising that a revised English translation had been uploaded into e-court under doc ID 0049-1779-ET-1. The Chamber hereby instructs the Registry to replace the translation of Exhibit P7072 with a revised one and gives the Defence one week from today to revisit the matter. And since I'm almost done, although the witness has arrived, I briefly deal with P6921, that is the reassignment of an exhibit number. On the 17th November of last year, 2014, during the testimony of Milos Milincic, P6921 was reserved for document bearing 65 ter number 02366a which is an excerpt from transcript from the RS Assembly. Additional pages were used with Vojo Kupresanin on the 11th and the 16th of December. On the 4th of November, 2015, the Prosecution e-mailed the Chamber and the Defence advising that it had uploaded all excerpts of this document into e-court as document bearing Rule 65 ter number 02366b. The Chamber hereby instructs the Registry to assign exhibit number P6921 to the new document and admits it into evidence, and the Defence has one week from today to revisit that matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There's one left. We will postpone that until later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Apologies, Mr. Kovac, for not paying proper attention to you entering the courtroom. Mr. Weber, are you ready to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kovac, I, however, have to remind that you you're still bound by the solemn declaration that you've given at the beginning of your testimony. Mr. Weber, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Kovac.

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Last Thursday, at transcript page 41317 to 18, you indicated that you interviewed General Grubac and Milenko Lalovic as sources of information for your report. General Radovan Grubac was the commander of the Herzegovina Corps of the VRS; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the commander of the Herzegovina Corps, and Lalovic is a colonel. Maybe I misheard that you called him general.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: We'll go one by one. Let's go in order, though. Novica Gusic was the commander of the Nevesinje Brigade of the Herzegovina Corps; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Grubac was the commander of the Herzegovina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes. Sir, please listen to my questions carefully. Novica Gusic was the commander of the Nevesinje Brigade of the Herzegovina Corps; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Novica Gusic. But I said I talked to Colonel Milenko Lalovic, commander of a battalion in that brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: During the war, Milenko Lalovic was a battalion commander in the Nevesinje Brigade; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 33245 for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, your microphone is on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I'm going to go through a set of documents and then ask you some questions. This is a 27 June 1992 regular combat report from General Grubac to the VRS Main Staff. In item 2, related to the combat readiness of the corps, the report states: "The Nevesinje Brigade is 'cisti' the area along the Podvelezje line and taking measures to seize the Velez feature." Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 33246 for the witness. This is a 28 June 1992 regular combat report from General Grubac to the VRS Main Staff. In item 2, related to the combat readiness of the corps, the report states: "The principal task of the Nevesinje Brigade is still to ciscenje Podvelezje and Velez feature." My question: The Nevesinje Brigade was carrying out operations near the town of Nevesinje and the Velez feature in late 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was not an operation. Those were regular combat activities in the area of responsibility of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: These activities were being carried out by a brigade under General Grubac's command; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he was not the brigade commander. Or maybe I'm getting the wrong interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I'll re-ask my question. These activities were being carried out by a brigade under General Grubac's command; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have P7657 for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: This is a list of imprisoned individuals from the area of Velez mountain on 26 June 1992. On this list there are 26 women and 20 children, the youngest of which was a baby that was seven days old.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have the last page of both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: At the end of the document, there's information that 30 persons from the list have been identified and buried and there are 42 persons that have not yet been found. In preparation for your report, did General Grubac or Milenko Lalovic tell you how they cleansed these areas of Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Objection; misstates the evidence, misstates the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If there's any issue about misstating a document, Mr. Weber, would you please quote it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I've gone to the two documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Did General Grubac or Mr. Lalovic tell you how they ciscenje'd these areas?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All this is taken out of the context a little. Even that term "cleansing" is in quotation marks. It does not relate to population. It relates to inserted groups and the mountain that was important to both Serbs and Muslims in that area. And the whole context of this document is being associated with ethnic cleansing of the population, which was not the case. They did not tell me about such things, nor did we discuss such things.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 33487 for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: This is a 14 June 1992 Nevesinje Brigade report from Colonel Novica Gusic. Under item 3 of the report, he informs the Herzegovina command that "measures should be taken immediately with the aim of moving out the population from the brigade's area of responsibility and especially Croatian and Muslim population because this has a negative effect on the mood and morale of units." Sir, the fact is that when the brigade was carrying out the ciscenje of villages, they were moving out Muslim and Croatian populations; right?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so. I think this is a one-sided view of the situation three months after the start of the civil war. I said yesterday that the people, all the three nations - Muslim, Croats, and Serbs - followed their armies wherever they controlled some territory, and these are the initial months of the civil war in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The Prosecution tenders 65 ter numbers 33245, 33246, and 33487 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 33245 receives exhibit number P7664. 65 ter number 33246 receives exhibit number P7665. And 65 ter number 33487 receives exhibit number P7666, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: All three are admitted into evidence. Could I ask one clarifying question. You said this is a one-sided view. Did you mean the view expressed in the document or the view as you apparently heard it in the question put to you by Mr. Weber?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I meant the attitude to this specific situation and the time of these events in that area. Because what is shown here is the moving of only one part of the population, Muslims and Croats, from the area of the Nevesinje Brigade. What is not seen is that this was a process in both directions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, I'm not asking you to elaborate on that. You said it was a one-sided view. Were you referring to the view expressed in the document, or were you referring to the view which you apparently heard in the question of Mr. Weber?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I meant it was a one-sided view compared to the objective situation on the ground at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's still not an answer to my question. But please move on, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: According to the first page of your curriculum vitae, you were a lead researcher at the Art of War Institute between September 1991 and September 1999. Did you hold this position in the JNA and then in the Yugoslav army, also known as the VJ?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I held that position at the institute in both those periods.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes. Were you a part of the JNA and then the VJ when you held that position -- those positions?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In your CV, I don't see any reference to your deployments to Croatia after September 1991 or to Bosnia in 1993. You do not include these deployments in the description of your professional career; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's included in the part that lists the duties within the troops. It says that I was commander of an artillery battalion, and, after that, Chief of Staff of an artillery regiment. I also said that I was sent for temporary work in the duration of six months without -- without abandoning my duties at the institute and that was subject to a legal arrangement.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: You were deployed to the Croatian Krajina in the fall of 1991 as part of the 145th Light Infantry Brigade, known as the Plaski Brigade; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, in that brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The commander of the 145th Brigade was Petar Trbovic; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution, please, have 65 ter 14406 for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While we're waiting for that, I have one follow-up question on one of the previous matters. Witness, you said when we looked at that document, paragraph 3, well, the population wanted to follow their armies. That's what the situation was but the document says otherwise. The document doesn't say, We should facilitate the Muslims and the Croats to follow their armies. But they say, We should take measures to remove them because they have a negative effect on the mood and the morale of the unit. That's something entirely different. Would you agree with me that that is not consistent with the earlier explanation you gave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think, Your Honours, that it is consistent, because these are events of the three months after the beginning of the war. The people moved all the time, and the whole first year of the civil war, people went to areas controlled by their own armies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But the document says something different. The document says, We should take measures to move them out because they have a negative effect on the mood and the morale of the units. That's something different. I mean, whether right or wrong, I leave that alone. But I still have difficulties in understanding how you consider this to be consistent with, if I understand you well, a kind of spontaneous movement of populations.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the most part, people moved spontaneously, but this specific measure shown in the act is not an intention to remove the population. Instead -- I don't know how to describe it. It's the beginning of the war, when that population too could have been endangered by paramilitaries, by neighbours. The spiral of mutual revenge and conflict was continuous in that area, especially during the Second World War. It's difficult to understand for somebody who is not closely associated by history to that area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That may all be true. I was focussing on what I read in this document. Do you find any support in this document for your view on what may have happened?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, to avoid any confusion, I believe the witness might be looking at a different document now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's the document which we had on our screen, and I think I quoted it almost literally a second ago. It was paragraph 3 of that document. If you want to look at it again, then we'll put it on the screen again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. Could I please have that document. And, if possible, could the question be more precise in relation to this third paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honours, it was 65 ter 33487, which I believe has now been admitted as Exhibit P7666.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What I asked you is that the whole of your explanation of people moving and what may have been the reasons, being in danger, et cetera, whether you find any support for that in the text of this document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think so, if one knows in detail what the situation was in that area and at this time when the civil war started.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, I'm asking you -- you have explained all that. I'm asking you whether you find any support for your views in the text of this document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Indirectly, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In a way which involves knowing the interethnic situation on the ground and relations there. And this was given rise to two or three years before the war and especially when the civil war started, and already 35.000 Serbs were moved out of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, I'll look whether what you tell us now is found in the text of the document, yes or no. Please proceed, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 14406 for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: This is a Korenica SDB security service Official Note about the attack on Saborsko on 12 November 1991. First of all, Plaski is located just to the north of Saborsko; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is where it is located.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The Official Note indicates that the attack included the Plaski TO, Territorial Defence, and units of the JNA. In the second paragraph, there's discussion of the ciscenje of houses and the remaining terrain that followed the attack. The last sentence of the paragraph states: "Today, the 13th of this month, we have continued 'ciscenje' the remaining terrain villages and inhabitants." Your brigade participated in this attack; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That period is one month before I arrived, and I don't have any precise knowledge about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. You agree that ciscenje of inhabitants includes civilians; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What the signatory of the document meant by that word is something that I don't know. Whether he meant that forces, armed forces, that were there should be driven out or whether he was referring to the inhabitants, the civil population there, that is what I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. I put it to you that you were deployed to areas of Croatia around the time in which villages were being ciscenje'd or inhabitants were being removed from villages in the Croatian Krajina; right?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. When we arrived as members of the JNA, there was a precisely defined front line between the two warring parties. As for all of these developments, the cleansing of the Serb and Croat populations on both sides of the front line, that was already over.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The Prosecution tenders 65 ter 14406 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 14406 receives exhibit number P7667, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P7667 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm about to go into other document and this is an okay time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, then we take the break first. Witness, we'd like to see you back in 20 minutes. We'll resume at 25 minutes to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I can use this time to address a housekeeping matter. It's with respect to D1357 marked for identification. This is the manual from the United Kingdom, JSP 383. The Defence was kind enough to send a full version to the Prosecution yesterday evening, and the Prosecution has had the opportunity to review it. We have no objection to the admission of the manual, provided that the cover page and chapter 5 is what's admitted. If the Defence could upload that, then we have no objection to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, cover page, chapter 5, is that -- oh, Mr. Ivetic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We will do that, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then once it's uploaded, you'll inform us and then we'll decide on admission. Please proceed, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 00743.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Kovac, this is a 18 May 1992 2nd Military District request for officers. The document is from General Mladic. You are listed as the second person on the list; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can see in the document, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Did you know General Mladic before May 1992?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew of his existence. I didn't know him personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Were you still deployed in Croatia at this time?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that is the period until the arrival of UNPROFOR. I don't know the exact date. It is possible that I was still there or that I was returning from Croatia, so that period. But in May, I did return from Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Where were you between May 1992 and the beginning of 1993?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the institute. The Institute of warfare, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: You were in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The Prosecution tenders 65 ter 743 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document number 743 receives exhibit number P7668, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Actually, Your Honours, if we're going to be talking about the list of names, I think the list of names and ranks, at least the portion relied upon, should be translated since in the English I see we don't have that. We just have the generic list of 14 names and the ranks without information that's being discussed by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do agree with you, that it's not there, and though the Chamber meanwhile thinks that it knows what a pukovnik is, for example, but if it's -- of course, we'll send it for further -- we'll ask the Prosecutor to send it for further translation. At the same time, if it's only about Mr. Kovac which you want to deal with it, then it looks as if it's artillery captain first class, which is -- that's at least how I understand it. If that's it, we could perhaps save the effort. But if you think it's relevant and important for us to know what the ranks of all the others are, then we'll certainly invite the Prosecution to do so. Mr. Ivetic, you think we should know what Mr. Risic and all the others, what their ranks are?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. You left it saying if the Prosecution wishes to rely upon it. I don't know what the Prosecution wishes to rely upon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you only want to rely on the Mitar Kovac entry. Is there anything else, Mr. Weber?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution has tendered many similar lists like this where I believe it is clear what it is. I think it would fall under the category of there were many requests for lists of officers from the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So if it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: -- so the quantity might be relied upon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's not an answer to the question. Do you want to rely on the ranks of all the other persons mentioned?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: We could possibly do that as a part of a larger group of exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. So you will send it for a full translation. Please proceed. Oh, yes, it should be MFI-ed, Madam Registrar. You've assigned a number already. Yes. That's P7668 which is now marked for identification, pending translation -- I should say pending full translation. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Kovac, when you were deployed as part of the Herzegovina Corps in 1993, you still received payments from the VJ; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that period, yes, because I hadn't handed over my duty yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: At transcript page 41295, you indicated that you served as an artillery officer in the VRS between January and August 1993. You were in the Herzegovina Corps during Operation Mac and Operation Lukavac 93; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Just during Operation Lukavac 93.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: During Operation Lukavac 93, the Herzegovina Corps captured Mount Treskavica, Mount Bjelasnica, and Mount Visocica; correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think you should repeat the names slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mount Treskavica, Mount Bljesnica, and part of Mount Visocica. This is what happened during Operation Lukavac 93, correct, from the Herzegovina Corps end?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only the Herzegovina Corps, also acting in concert with part of the forces of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. And it's not that it was taken. Rather, this territory was returned, territory that had been taken by the Muslim forces a year before that, in 1992. So it liberated the area that had previously been taken by the Muslim forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: From 1999 until 2014, the primary focus of your work pertained to strategic planning and the development of national defence policies in the Republic of Serbia; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. From 1999 until 2004, I was head of a department in the mentioned institute, and I was involved in leading research projects that are listed in the CV. As from 2004 onwards, I was appointed chief of Department for Strategic planning in the Ministry of Defence in the sector for defence policy.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your research and publications between 1999 and 2014 related to your work as a member of the Ministry of Defence and the military institute in Serbia; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not only at the military institute. While I was at the institute, yes, that is until 2004. And then after that, research work was in the form of teaching at the Military Academy, later on at the University of Defence. And it was carried out within projects of some of the schools of Belgrade university or rather faculties of the University of Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Did you say between 1999 and 2004 or 2014?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: 2014. Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And I could have done both for the Ministry of Defence and military institute.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: You mentioned your book, "History of the Art of War," and the fact that there were multiple volumes. Your co-authors of this publication on different volumes were Janacka Sarakovic [phoen] and Bozidar Forca?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Forca.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only they. So you found these three names somewhere but there were eight researchers in that period, that five-year period. Most of them were involved in the first monograph that pertained to the period until 1920. I had the role of project leader and I --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: If we can just continue. You've explained a lot of this already. In fact, most of your articles and publications were with a group of co-authors; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Most of them are author publications, single-author publications.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: You wrote an article entitled: "Military Aspects of NATO Aggression on the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia" with Bozidar Forca, which was published in 2000?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: This is one of the articles that you do not mention in your CV; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I said that it's about 135 articles and that I had only provided some of them in my CV.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I return to your book.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 33492a.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We don't have the corresponding -- yes, there it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: This is one of your publications concerning the History of Military Arts, the one that you co-authored with Colonel Forca; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could we actually please return to the first page. I see it's uploaded out of order.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: One of the consulting editors on this publication was General Radovan Radinovic; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please go to page 4 in both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: This is the section of the book on military control. In the first paragraph, you describe the continuous interconnected cycle in which military control is exercised; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: You describe the five functions that are mutually causal and continuous. They are, first, planning; second, organisation; third, commanding, issuing orders; fourth, co-ordination; and, fifth, control. A commander exercises military control over forces under their command through the continuous performance of these functions; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not a new classification of functions. These functions of command and control go back to the classics, to the present day, so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In the next paragraph you discuss the role of the commander and state: "The commander was considered to be the main actor in commanding who had the exclusive right to make decisions and issue orders." I'm just going to pause here. General Mladic, as the commander of the VRS, possessed the exclusive right to make decisions and issue orders; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that are you comparing the wrong period from this book to something that happened in 1990 onwards. This, from the book, is from 1920 until 1945. These are generalisations of theoretical and empirical knowledge that primarily has to do with the Second World War.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Doctrinally speaking, and you've described how these are very well-known things, General Mladic, as the commander of the VRS, possessed the exclusive right to make decisions and issue orders; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Misstates the evidence. General Mladic was not the commander of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: He was appointed to the commander of the Army of Republika Srpska on 12 May 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's evidence given by you at this moment, but I think what Mr. Ivetic may be pointing at is that the president of the Republika Srpska is the Commander-in-Chief or the supreme commander. Let's not -- I mean, we know what we're talking about, more or less, and that you are referring to General Mladic in his position as the --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Commander --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- commander, not the Commander-in-Chief perhaps. But let's -- I mean, is there any dispute about these matters? If not, let's then move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, if we're talking about a military expert or trying to use expertise, being precise is important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The witness is present and he does understand --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please rephrase your question using the right terminology.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: First of all, you agree that the commander of an army has the exclusive right to make decisions and issue orders; right?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the case in every army of the world. He has the exclusive right to make decisions within his powers.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The rest of the sentence indicates that the commander could transfer part of his powers and responsibilities with respect to issuing orders to his assistants, which did not exclude his liability for a successful realisation of his duties. In other words, a commander can delegate some duties but they are still responsible for the tasks to be carried out; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would kindly ask you to separate the findings from monographs until 1995 and your specific questions about General Mladic. In this period, General Mladic was not born or was a child.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: The year was 1945, not 1995.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is not fair to compare something from the period of up to 1945.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time we have a lot of other doctrinal stuff in. The Prosecution would just tender 65 ter 33492a into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 33492a receives exhibit number P7669, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Did you write the report entitled: "Report on the Command Authority of General Ratko Mladic in the War in Bosnia and Herzegovina"?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Did you personally author each of the paragraphs of the report?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he personally -- I personally authored it. But in the footnotes, there are things that I took over from other documents and expert reports, as I mentioned in the previous days.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: You're saying the contents of the report are a product of your own analysis and work.

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Are there any paragraphs in your report where you significantly borrow text from another source without attributing either the conclusions or the text to the other source?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are no such documents. Passages are marked where they contain positions taken based on some other analysis or document, and I listed the expert reports that I used the most, both from the Defence side and the Prosecution side.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 1D05358. If we could please go to page 177 of the B/C/S and page 179 of the English translation. If we could please focus on paragraph 4.220.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: This is your report in this case. You discussed a number of things in paragraph 4.220, including the murder of two young Sarajevans on 19 May 1993. Focussing your attention on the sentence starting on the third line from the bottom of the page in the B/C/S with the words "prvo je na mostu smrtno pogodjen Bosko." [Phoen] In the English, the sentence starts: "First Bosko was shot dead on the bridge." Do you see this part of the paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could I have the next page in both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: You continue your discussion of the facts related to this event up until the phrase "Emir prenesena na groblje Lav u Sarajevu," [phoen], which is translated in the English as "the Lav cemetery in Sarajevo as Emir's parents wished"; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: You do not attribute any of this information to Wikipedia, do you?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not only from Wikipedia. It's from several sources, cross-referenced information, and the one that was closest to me is stated in the footnote, as you can see here from the newspaper Slobodna Dalmacija, Free Dalmatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could we please leave the B/C/S version on the screen and bring up 65 ter 33486 next to the report. If we could please focus on the highlighted portion.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Kovac, before you is a highlighted version of the B/C/S Wikipedia page for the Romeo and Juliet murders in Sarajevo from sr.wikipedia.org. Could you please focus on the highlighted part that starts with the phrase "prvo je na mostu" [phoen] through the sentence that ends "Lav u Sarajevu." You borrowed this text from Wikipedia for your report; right?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, from -- it's from Slobodna Dalmacija.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Well, the only part of the text that is different from your report is a single phrase, "su se obe stranje u subukobu," [phoen], meaning both parties of the conflict. It appears that you have changed this phrase to "su se Srbi i Muslimani," [phoen], which is translated as "while Serbs and Muslims." That's the only difference between this Wikipedia text and the text in your report; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a paraphrase of the text based on the source of Slobodna Dalmacija, as stated in the footnote.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, the one source that's actually cited in this Wikipedia page is from Mr. Emin Garaplija and the same interview publication which you have in footnote 484 of paragraph 4.220. The Wikipedia page is where you got your source; right?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not right. It's the newspaper Slobodna Dalmacija.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, have you checked the Slobodna Dalmacija source?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I am aware of it but I see that it's also listed right here on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But you are more or less suggesting to the witness that he copied it from Wikipedia. There is, of course, a possibility - and that's the reason why I'm asking you - that Wikipedia has copied from Slobodna Dalmacija which then might result in the same text to be found on Wikipedia compared to what is found in the witness's report. Have you considered that, and would you please in the following questions or perhaps tomorrow pay attention that it's a possibility as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You have considered it?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I am aware of the source. I will, of course, proceed accordingly tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: One other observation. The footnote should be 464.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Are you aware that Mr. Garaplija has made a variety of claims after his 1997 conviction for maltreating Nedzad Herenda, and do you realise these theories or many of these claims have been rejected by courts in Bosnia, including the Human Rights Chamber of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've read many texts, both from the press and monographs related to this case, and I formed my own opinion based on all that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. Are you aware that his claims have been rejected by courts in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Did you review all of the source materials referenced in the footnotes of your report?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Just to finish off today with a couple of general questions. You stated that you had a talk with Nenad Petrusic about the scope of your work and the material that is available for your report. What specifically did you understand the scope of your report to be?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I did not think of the physical scope. I thought more about the structure of the report that should cover the key issues related to the civil war in Bosnia-Herzegovina and primarily in the territory of the Sarajevo theatre of war and the protected areas of Srebrenica and Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. In our review of the source materials referenced in your report, we found that you often appeared to have drawn upon the analysis of Radovan Radinovic. We see that -- we counted up that General Radinovic is the most commonly referenced source in your report, and there appears to be at least 84 references to his previous reports; correct? He is the most commonly referred to person in your report; right?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most frequently I referred to that one, but I referred also to Butler, Butler's reports. Mostly I used General Radinovic, and that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In comparing your report and General Radinovic's reports, we appear to find a significant number of paragraphs where the text, conclusions and analysis were substantially similar or the same as General Radinovic's but where there were no references to one of General Radinovic's reports. Mr. Kovac, with the Chamber's permission, I'm going to hand you a document that lists some examples of overlapping paragraphs where it is not apparent to us that you cite General Radinovic. I have courtesy copies for the Chamber and the Defence. And just if we could describe it quickly. Each one on the list contains entries with paragraph numbers from your report and paragraph numbers from one of General Radinovic's reports. I also have available B/C/S hard copies of General Radinovic's reports so you can compare them to your report.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Again, with Your Honours' leave, after court today, I'd like to give the witness the four binders of the reports and ask the witness to compare the listed paragraphs from his report to the corresponding paragraphs from General Radinovic's reports. I can then ask further questions once the witness has looked at this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, the binders of which reports, of the Radinovic's reports?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: They are the -- the four binders each contain the separate Radinovic reports in each one and they are listed on the -- and they're provided on the list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Before we ask the witness to do a lot of homework, Mr. Weber apparently puts it to you that you many, many portions of your report are similar in text with the Radinovic's reports without a reference to those reports. Do you agree with that, or do you disagree?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am not talking in advance about any specific paragraph or passage. I'll first have to consult this. But wherever I explicitly expressed positions identical to the analysis of General Radinovic, I referred to the source and provided a footnote.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The issue, however, is - and that's apparently what Mr. Weber puts to you - that where you do not perhaps explicitly express positions which -- but that you adopt more or less the text as we find it in these other reports, without a clear reference to the Radinovic's reports. Do you allow for the possibility that you have done that in so many instances? And briefly counting, I think we're talking about some 30 or more paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's possible that where a footnote is given, it relates to two or three paragraphs, especially if they were reformulated or commented in my own way because it's the same substance, the same event, the same documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, you're putting this to the witness. You're apparently tried to analyse it. Are we talking about similar language? Are we talking about 90, 95 per cent of the words the same? Are we talking about 40 per cent? Or 70 per cent? Could you give us an impression as --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I would say over 75 per cent of the words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of the words. Then we are talking verbatim about the words used in the same order.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Substantially the same, yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Witness for 30 or more paragraphs as listed here, would you agree that your text would, for 75 per cent, be verbatim, the same, as the Radinovic reports where you have not footnoted Mr. Radinovic's report or reports?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The source is stated in the way that I said. If the paragraphs were reformulated and expressed in my own way, then there is no footnote. And in the sense of value --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Even if 75 per cent of the text remains identical to the one in Mr. Radinovic's report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't see a problem if even that percentage is true, if the same words were used, considering that it's the same event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I was not asking whether you see a problem in it. I'm just trying to just establish what we are talking about. Are you willing to compare it and to see whether you agree that for those paragraphs, that substantially the same text is used as by Mr. Radinovic? Are you willing to compare that overnight so that we hear from you tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I will compare them. I said at the outset that that analysis and Butler's analysis were the primary sources I used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Have you similarly quoted? That means used the same words from the Butler reports as well in a similar way; that is, 75 per cent of a paragraph using the same words as we find them in Mr. Butler's report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When a passage or a paragraph was cited, it could have been the same, 40, 50 or 70 per cent. The substance was expressed in the same way and a footnote was provided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And also without a footnote? Because I do understand that Mr. Weber is pointing at those paragraphs where, quite substantially, text is the same as in the Radinovic report but without a footnote. Have you similarly adopted major parts of the text of Mr. Butler's reports without footnoting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Footnotes were given and even my comment was added, or a clarification of that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then you're invited to work overnight on -- Mr. Ivetic, would you still want to have a look at the binders before they are given to Mr. Kovac?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I would, especially since I'm surprised that they cover four binders. That doesn't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I take it that the parties will look at the binders and see whether there's any disagreement on that, and once they've done so, that it be given to the VWS so as to provide them to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm prepared to do that, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, Witness, you'll later receive the binders with the reports of Mr. Radinovic, and you're invited to compare on the basis of this list whether, indeed, you have adopted a large portion, and you heard Mr. Weber talking about some 75 per cent minimal, of his text in your report without a specific footnote in that paragraph to the Radinovic reports. If you'd like -- if you'd do that, we would appreciate to hear from you tomorrow. Because we'll adjourn for the day, and we will resume tomorrow, Wednesday, the 18th of November, though we do not need you right in the beginning because we'll first hear the evidence of another witness, which most likely takes approximately one hour and a half, I think. Mr. Lukic? Mr. Ivetic? I don't know who to address because we have a videolink tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the conversation with the Prosecution, we think that we might finish tomorrow's first witness in the first session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You mean the Defence or the whole of the testimony?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The whole of the testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The whole of the testimony. Then could you please take care that you are standing by here in this building from quarter to 11.00. That would -- and I again instruct you that you should not speak or communicate with whomever about your testimony, whether already given or still to be given. If that's all clear to you, you may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's all clear. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We adjourn for the day, and with our apologies to those assisting us going beyond the time, we resume tomorrow, Wednesday, the 18th of November, 2015, 9.30 in the morning, in this same courtroom, I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 18th day of November, 2015, at 9.30 a.m. 20 21 22 23 24 25
